teaser: In 1716 her princely patron died. Rachel Ruysch, 52 and mother of ten, simply kept painting.

lesson.text: In June 1716, Rachel Ruysch lost the best job a painter in Europe could have. For eight years she had been court painter to Johann Wilhelm, the Elector Palatine, a German prince in Düsseldorf. He paid her a yearly salary, bought much of what she painted, and let her stay home in Amsterdam. That month he died.

She was 52. She had given birth to ten children, and her husband, the portrait painter Juriaen Pool, earned far less than she did. The date on this picture is 1716, the year the salary stopped. If she was worried, the painting does not show it. It is as sure-handed as anything she ever made.
Ruysch's flower pieces sold for 750 to 1,250 guilders each. Rembrandt, in his lifetime, rarely received more than 500 for a painting.

Her training explains the confidence. Her father, Frederik Ruysch, was Amsterdam's professor of anatomy and botany, and she grew up among dried plants, pinned insects and specimens in jars. At 15 she was apprenticed to Willem van Aelst, a leading flower painter. He taught her to break with the neat, round, symmetrical bouquet.
Nothing here is centered. Trace how the bouquet moves.

lines.label: The S-curve
lines.text: From the rose lying on the marble, the brightest blooms wind upward to the iris at the top. Your eye travels a long, lazy S, as if the bouquet were still growing.

lines.label: The shadow side
lines.text: The right half sinks into gloom. Dark leaves and half-lit flowers trail down toward the table. Ruysch lights only part of the bouquet and lets the rest go.

lines.label: The marble edge
lines.text: The tabletop is the one calm, straight line. It ends before the right edge of the picture, so the dark background slips down behind it.

lesson.text: That uneven light is her drama. The white, salmon and pink flowers at the heart seem to push out of the darkness toward you, while others are sensed more than seen. It makes a small picture, under half a meter tall (about 19 inches), feel deep.
Ruysch joined two kinds of knowledge that rarely met: a scientist's accuracy about every petal and insect, and an artist's freedom to arrange them into movement.

The scientist's side shows in the population. This bouquet is alive with small animals, each one drawn precisely enough to be identified, and none of them placed by accident. Wander through it and you will meet them.

spots.title: A beetle at work
spots.text: A brown beetle climbs across a white petal blotched with dark red. Ruysch gives it legs, feelers and a faint shadow.

spots.title: The blue fly
spots.text: A fat fly with a metallic blue body sits on the outer petals of the pink rose. Flies gather where things begin to spoil: a quiet hint that this beauty is brief.

spots.title: Wings in the dark
spots.text: A small dark butterfly spotted with orange hovers by a flower bud at the upper left, almost lost against the background.

spots.title: Long feelers
spots.text: On the right end of the marble slab, an insect with very long antennae walks toward the edge. You only find it once your eyes adjust to the shadow.

spots.title: The iris
spots.text: A pale iris with purple-veined lower petals crowns the bouquet. It leans to the right, off the central axis, which sets the whole arrangement tilting.

spots.title: The window
spots.text: Below the flowers, the dark glass vase carries a small bright reflection of a window with panes. It is the only glimpse of her workroom.

spots.title: The fallen rose
spots.text: A pink rose lies on the marble, turned toward us. It starts the S-curve, and it is also a flower that has already left the water.

spots.title: Her name
spots.text: In the dark below the table edge, in faint flowing script: Rachel Ruysch, and the year 1716. She kept her own surname all her life.

lesson.text: Her father was famous across Europe for his cabinet of preserved specimens, which he arranged into elaborate displays. In 1717, the year after this painting, he sold the entire collection to Tsar Peter the Great of Russia.

And the lost salary? She did not need it. Collectors kept buying, and she went on painting for three more decades. On her last pictures, made in her eighties, she proudly added her age next to her signature. She died in 1750 at 86, and poets published a volume of verse in her honor.
In 1723 Ruysch and her husband won the top prize in a Dutch lottery: 75,000 guilders, a fortune. She could have retired on the spot. She carried on painting anyway.

One thing to keep from 1716, then. For most artists of her time, losing a prince meant ruin. For Ruysch it was a change of customers. She had built something sturdier than a patron: a name that buyers trusted on sight.

quiz.question: What happened to Rachel Ruysch in 1716?
options: Her patron, the Elector Palatine, died
She stopped painting for ten years
quiz.explanation: Johann Wilhelm died in June 1716, ending her post as his court painter.

quiz.question: What did her teacher Willem van Aelst encourage her to abandon?
quiz.explanation: He taught her asymmetrical arrangements that seem to move.

quiz.question: What shape do the brightest flowers trace through the picture?
quiz.explanation: From the fallen rose to the iris, the lit blooms wind upward in an S.

quiz.question: How did Ruysch's prices compare with Rembrandt's?
options: They were about a tenth of his
quiz.explanation: Her flower pieces fetched 750 to 1,250 guilders; Rembrandt rarely got more than 500.

quiz.question: What did her father do?
options: He was a court portrait painter
He was a professor of anatomy and botany
quiz.explanation: Frederik Ruysch taught anatomy and botany and kept a famous cabinet of specimens.

facts.text: Ruysch worked as court painter to a German prince without leaving Amsterdam.
facts.explanation: The Elector Palatine in Düsseldorf let her stay at home and send him her work.

facts.text: After winning a lottery fortune in 1723, Ruysch gave up painting.
facts.explanation: She kept working and signed pictures with her age well into her eighties.

facts.text: The bouquet is lit evenly from edge to edge.
facts.explanation: Only the center glows; the right side sinks into shadow.
